Here, you'll find the virtual companion to all of our hands-on workshops for the semester. These will be the same as your physical hand-outs, but I know many folks prefer to have them up on their screens as they work through the activities.

The purpose of these workshops is to practice applying the topics that we discuss in lecture using real-world examples and data. The associated data files for each lab are linked in the `Frontmatter` section atop each page (all the files are also located [here](link%20here)). Over the semester, we'll explore some of the frustrations and challenges of working with bio/ecological data (of which there are many!), but together we'll conquer them, setting y'all up for success in analyzing, interpreting, and sharing your own data.

A total of 8 of the workshops will have an assignment/report that will be peer reviewed (i.e., evaluated). The first three to four weeks will be devoted to a primer of using R/RStudio, basic programming, project management, and the use of Git and GitHub (which we will use extensively in this class to manage course materials and feedback).

## Downloading, installing, and setting up R and RStudio

For this course, we'll be using R and R Studio to do all of our work. You also have the option of using the Posit Cloud service for workshops and assignments. It's essentially an online virtual machine to run RStudio in your browser. This will avoid version issues, package incompatibilities, and Mac vs Windows challenges that you might otherwise face. This is a paid service we'll be using for class and it will expire after our semester concludes, so I also encourage you to install R and R Studio on your own machines if you haven't already. Click on the buttons below to install both R (the language, or engine that enables our analyses to be performed) and RStudio (the shell, or vessel that the engine of R sits in and gives us the nifty features to manage files, version history, and write pretty and readable code).

## Completing and submitting workshop reports

In labs, we'll be writing code in a couple of different ways, but primarily what I will be recommending is using an R Notebook to write, annotate, and interpret your code. R Notebooks are a type of Markdown file where we can mix formatted text, code chunks, and a whole bunch of other goodies. R Notebooks help to organize your code into sections and subsections, and will let you write about the output directly in the document rather than creating a Word document (shudder...). We'll go through this a bit more in the first lab, but take a look at the following links to learn a bit more about R Notebooks and R Markdown.

- [Writing code in R notebooks](https://bookdown.org/yihui/rmarkdown/notebook.html)
- [R Notebook (Markdown) cheatsheet](https://posit.co/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/rmarkdown-1.pdf)

### Report submission protocol

1.  **Complete your report:** Follow the instructions for the workshop and complete your work as a `.qmd` document. Format it appropriately (should be structured, easy-to-follow and your various sections should make clear links to the workshop prompts).
2.  **Stage and commit your changes:** Once you're done with your report, stage and commit your changes locally using an informative commit message.
3.  **Push your changes to GitHub:** Push your changes into your personal course repository.
4.  **Create an issue and assign your reviewer:** In your repository, select the <kbd>Issues</kbd> tab. From there, select <kbd>New issue</kbd>.
    - Enter a consistent title for each week's submission using this format: `wX_workshop_report` where you replace X with the current week.
    - See my [example issue here](https://github.com/entomology-3927-5927/hemberger-jeremy-3927/issues/1), and format your issue text similarly. Feel free to add notes to your reviewer (e.g., highlighting areas where you'd like specific feedback or struggled), and include a funny image, meme, or gif because we all need laughs these days. Be sure to tag your reviewer using the `@` sign and selecting their username. Reviewer assignments for each week are posted on the X
5.  **Complete your peer review** See below for the rubric and suggestions. Remember to be both kind and constructive. No one likes a [Reviewer #2](https://patthomson.net/2026/06/01/how-to-be-reviewer-2/).
6. **Close the issue:** Once you have completed your peer review, post it, and then mark the issue as "closed". 

### Peer review rubric

Your job when peer reviewing your colleagues code can be distilled down to one basic task: **your job is to review the code as if you were going to use it in 3-6 months without the author sitting next to you.** Ask yourself:

- Can you understand what it does?
- Can you understand why it does it?
- Can you reproduce the results of your colleague?

This big picture framing is far more helpful in directing someone to make changes to increase reproducibility rather than just being nitpicky on syntax and code style. That said, obviously make suggestions about smaller changes you think would be important to implement, but don't get lost in the sauce: try and focus on the big-picture.

Criteria to keep in mind and a rubric to help shape your feedback. You don't need to use these scores, but feel free to borrow the classifications in your feedback.

| **Criterion** | **Excellent** | **Adequate** | **Needs improvement** |
|----------------|------------------------|----------------|-----------------|
| **1. Organization & readability** | Code is logically organized, easy to follow, and uses clear spacing/structure. | Mostly understandable but some sections are difficult to follow. | Code is difficult to follow or poorly organized. |
| **2. Naming & style** | Objects/variables have descriptive names and code follows consistent R style. | Names/style are generally understandable but inconsistent in places. | Names are unclear or style makes the code difficult to understand. |
| **3. Comments & documentation** | Comments explain the purpose/reasoning behind important steps without unnecessarily narrating the code. | Some useful comments, but important steps may be unexplained. | Little or no documentation. |
| **4. Use of R/tidyverse** | Uses appropriate functions efficiently; avoids unnecessary repetition. | Code works but could be simplified or made more efficient. | Code contains substantial unnecessary repetition or inappropriate approaches. |
| **5. Reproducibility** | Code runs from beginning to end with minimal intervention and clearly identifies required packages/data. | Mostly reproducible but requires some clarification or manual steps. | Difficult or impossible for another person to reproduce. |

::: callout-important
Be sure to try and highlight positives and not just negatives. What is one thing the author did particularly well? It's equally important to emphasize the positive aspects of our work in addition to critiquing what needs improvement.
:::
